# Lead-Time Compression Program
## From 14 Weeks to 6–7 Without Touching the Gates

*Prepared for the executive team. All week-counts and savings below are a working model built from typical make-to-order industrial equipment operations; Phase 0 exists to replace these estimates with measured data before any commitment is made.*

---

## 1. Core Diagnosis: You Are Losing Deals to Waiting, Not to Working

In equipment manufacturing with certified multi-stage inspection, actual touch time — machining, welding, assembly, testing — is typically **15–25% of quoted lead time**. The other 75–85% is queue, handoff, procurement wait, inspection scheduling, non-conformance loops, and documentation assembly. A competitor quoting 6 weeks against your 14 has almost certainly not found a way to machine steel four times faster. They have eliminated the white space between the work.

This distinction is the entire strategic foundation of the plan, because it explains the last failure:

**The previous compression attempt squeezed the work and the gates. This plan squeezes only the waiting.**

When leadership last demanded speed, the organization had no map of where time actually went — so the pressure landed on the visible activities: inspections were rushed or overlapped, testing was abbreviated, marginal dispositions were accepted, unproven suppliers were expedited in. The warranty spike two years later was the predictable result of compressing value-added and verification time on a process whose underlying first-pass yield was never fixed. The plan below is designed so that **no certified gate is shortened, skipped, or softened — gates are made to pass faster because fewer things fail them and nothing waits for them.**

---

## 2. Phase 0 (Weeks 1–6): Find Where the Time Actually Goes

Before changing anything, instrument the present. Three workstreams, run in parallel:

**2.1 Value-stream autopsy.** Pull the timestamps from 5–8 recently shipped orders (a mix of standard and configured units) and reconstruct every order hour-by-hour: quote → order entry → engineering release → each PO → material receipt → each operation → each inspection request → each inspection execution → each NCR raised/closed → test → data book → ship. Produce a verified decomposition of the 14 weeks.

**2.2 Quality forensics.** Root-cause the warranty spike from the last attempt: which failure modes, which process changes they correlate with, which gates were bypassed or pressured. Output is a codified **Red Lines list** (Section 5.5) — the specific practices that must never be repeated. This document is also the trust-reset artifact for the three feuding functions: it proves the failure was a *system* failure, not one department's fault.

**2.3 Product segmentation.** Split the catalog into (a) standard/repeat configurations, (b) configured variants, (c) engineer-to-order. The blanket 14-week quote almost certainly prices the worst case across all three — meaning you are quoting standard products as if they were custom. The competitor's 6 weeks is likely a standard-config number.

**Expected finding (hypothesis to validate):**

| Stage | Est. share of 14 wks | Primary loss mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Quote, order entry, engineering release | 2–3 wks | Serial spec-clarification loops with customer; custom engineering per order |
| Procurement (long-lead: castings, forgings, drives, special alloys) | 4–5 wks on critical path | POs placed only after order release; spot buys at supplier queue times |
| Fabrication & machining | 3 wks | Batch-and-queue; bottleneck machine; WIP piles between operations |
| Assembly | 1–2 wks | Kit shortages; waiting on late parts and rework loops |
| Inspection (wait + execute + NCR disposition) | 2–3 wks | Gates requested ad hoc; inspector queue; NCRs age days awaiting disposition |
| Final test, certification docs, ship prep | 1–2 wks | Data book assembled at the end; FAT/witness scheduling conflicts |
| Embedded buffer | ~1 wk | Distrust-driven sandbagging at every handoff |

If validated, roughly **8 of the 14 weeks are recoverable without accelerating a single value-added operation.**

---

## 3. The Compression Levers

### 3.1 Process & Flow
- **Value-stream cells for standard families.** Reorganize fabrication and assembly around product families to cut inter-department queues and transport; apply SMED changeover reduction at the bottleneck machine to enable smaller batches (smaller batches = shorter queues for everything behind them).
- **Kitting and supermarkets.** Assembly starts only on complete kits; a parts supermarket between machining and assembly eliminates the "wait for one missing bracket" stall that idles a nearly finished unit.
- **Freeze-point concurrent engineering.** Engineering and production overlap only at defined, quality-approved freeze points with formal design reviews — the disciplined version of what was done recklessly last time.
- **Error-proofing at defect-prone steps** (poka-yoke fixtures, torque verification interlocks, first-article checks) targeted at the specific failure modes from the warranty forensics.

### 3.2 Inventory & Product Architecture
- **Modularize and configure-to-order.** Redesign the standard line into pre-engineered modules built to stock; final assembly becomes configure-to-order. This is the single largest lever — it moves module fabrication *off* the order's critical path entirely and is the most common way competitors reach 6 weeks.
- **Strategic long-lead stock.** Carry castings, forgings, drives, and special alloys sized on demand variability and supplier reliability — not per-order purchasing. Use consignment or VMI where suppliers will accept it.
- **Blanket POs and reserved capacity** with key suppliers replace spot buys, converting your position in their queue from random to guaranteed.

### 3.3 Scheduling & Quoting
- **Quote from capacity, not from habit.** Replace the blanket 14 weeks with a finite-capacity scheduling model that quotes configuration-specific lead times from actual open slots. Standard configs get a fast lane; sales sees slot availability in near-real time. Expect immediate commercial impact: many of the lost one-in-three deals are standard units being quoted custom lead times.
- **Pre-booked quality gates.** Inspection slots — internal *and* third-party/certified witness points — are reserved at order release, exactly as machine capacity is reserved. Nothing waits for an inspector's calendar.
- **Pull scheduling with FIFO lanes** between departments; level the monthly load to kill the end-of-quarter hockey stick that wrecks both lead time and workmanship.
- **Bottleneck capacity audit.** If a machine, test bay, or inspection station is the constraint, add shift coverage there before anywhere else (an hour at the bottleneck is an hour of lead time; an hour elsewhere is nothing).

### 3.4 Suppliers
- **Certified supplier program.** Audit top suppliers so their certified inspection data is accepted in lieu of duplicate incoming inspection (dock-to-line). Status is earned, audited quarterly, and revocable — this *reduces* total inspection load while raising supplier quality.
- **Dual-source or near-source the longest-lead items**; qualify a second foundry/forge now, before you need it.
- **Lead-time SLAs with incentives** in contracts, plus supplier development help on their own setup and queue times.

---

## 4. Where the 8 Weeks Come From (Model)

| Lever cluster | Est. lead-time recovery |
|---|---|
| Front-end: standard config catalog, quote-from-capacity, freeze-point engineering | 1.5–2 wks |
| Procurement: long-lead stock + blanket POs + certified suppliers | 2.5–3 wks |
| Flow: cells, kitting, changeover reduction, bottleneck coverage | 1.5 wks |
| Quality flow: pre-booked gates, NCR fast-track, progressive documentation | 1.5–2 wks |
| Buffer release as reliability is proven | 0.5–1 wk |
| **Total** | **~8 wks → quoted 6–7 wks for standard configurations** |

Configured and engineer-to-order products land at 8–10 and 10–12 weeks respectively — still quote-competitive, since those buyers expect longer cycles.

---

## 5. Protecting the Quality Gates

This section is the license for the whole program. Five mechanisms:

**5.1 The gates are untouchable; the waiting is not.** Every certified hold point, witness point, and inspection stage remains, at full rigor, under the certification regime (ISO 9001, ASME/PED/ATEX/API as applicable, plus customer-specific requirements). Quality holds a **formal veto** over any change touching a certified gate. The compression targets the *queue in front of* each gate.

**5.2 Shift quality left.** The reason gates threaten schedules is that failures found at a gate trigger rework loops. Deploy operator self-verification with calibrated instruments, first-article inspection per setup, and SPC on key characteristics — so first-pass yield rises and gates become fast confirmations rather than discovery events. Track FPY per gate as a headline metric.

**5.3 Progressive documentation.** Build the certification data book *as the order flows*: material certs captured at receipt, weld maps at welding, test results at test. End-stage document assembly is typically 1–2 hidden weeks and a classic source of last-minute quality escapes — eliminate it structurally.

**5.4 NCR fast-track.** Daily triage stand-up for non-conformances with a Material Review Board holding pre-delegated disposition authority for standard cases and a 48-hour disposition SLA. NCR aging is pure lead time with zero quality benefit.

**5.5 Red Lines and tripwires.** The warranty-forensics output becomes an explicit never-again list (e.g., no ship-before-data-book-complete, no unqualified supplier substitution, no abbreviated test durations, no disposition under schedule pressure). Pair it with a **leading-indicator dashboard** — FPY per gate, NCR rate, overtime %, supplier defect PPM, test first-pass — reviewed weekly, with pre-defined tripwires that automatically pause compression activities if quality indicators move the wrong way. Warranty claims by ship-month are the trailing confirmation.

---

## 6. Aligning Production, Quality, and Sales

The feud is structural, not personal: **sales is paid on bookings** (so it overpromises), **production on utilization** (so it runs big batches and resists expedites), **quality on zero escapes** (so it adds buffers and rechecks). Each is behaving rationally against its own scorecard. Fix the scorecard:

- **One shared metric set.** All three functions carry the same four numbers: quoted lead time, on-time-in-full delivery, first-pass yield, and warranty rate. Tie 20–30% of variable compensation for all three leadership teams to this shared set. Local metrics (utilization, bookings) become secondary diagnostics, not goals.
- **Single accountable owner.** A value-stream manager (or the COO) owns quoted lead time end-to-end with authority across functions. Functional heads own capability; the value-stream owner owns the order's clock.
- **S&OP cadence.** Monthly sales-and-operations planning for demand/capacity/material alignment; a weekly 30-minute order-review with all three functions triaging the active order book, expedites, and gate schedules. Cross-functional daily tier meetings on the floor per product family.
- **Quote governance.** Sales quotes only from the capacity model; exceptions go to a deal desk with production and quality sign-off. This ends the "sales promised 8, we're set up for 14" conflict at the source — and gives sales something it has never had: a credible fast number for standard products.
- **Reframe quality's role.** Quality engineers are embedded in the flow redesign as co-designers of *fast* gates, not gatekeepers defending slow ones. The formal veto (5.1) is the key: empowered owners streamline; suspected blockers entrench.
- **Publish the Phase 0 forensics.** A blameless, fact-based account of the last failure — presented jointly by the three function heads — is the explicit trust-reset event that launches the program.

---

## 7. Phased Roadmap

| Phase | Timeline | Actions | Quoted lead time (standard configs) | Quality posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Diagnose** | Wks 1–6 | VSM autopsy, warranty forensics, segmentation, baseline metrics | 14 wks (unchanged) | Baseline FPY/NCR/warranty established |
| **1. Quick wins** | Wks 6–16 | Pre-booked gates, NCR fast-track, progressive documentation, quote-from-capacity, standard-config fast lane | **10–11 wks** | Zero gate changes; FPY dashboard live |
| **2. Structural** | Mo 4–9 | Modularization/CTO, long-lead stock, supplier certification & dual sourcing, finite scheduling, cell layout | **8 wks** | Every change passes PFMEA review + quality veto |
| **3. Optimize** | Mo 9–18 | SPC maturity, dock-to-line expansion, takt-based flow, digital thread/MES | **6–7 wks** | FPY and warranty at or better than pre-program baseline |

**Pilot discipline:** run Phases 1–2 on one product family first, holding the rest of the line on the current process as a control group. Scale only on evidence — measured lead time *and* stable quality indicators.

---

## 8. Success Metrics & Tripwires

| KPI | Baseline | 6-mo target | 18-mo target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quoted lead time, standard configs | 14 wks | 10–11 | 6–7 |
| On-time-in-full | (measure) | 90% | 95%+ |
| First-pass yield per gate | (measure) | +10 pts | +20 pts |
| NCR disposition time | (measure) | 48-hr SLA | 24 hr |
| Warranty claims per shipped unit | (measure) | Flat | Below baseline |
| Win rate on speed-contested deals | ~67% loss | — | Halve the loss rate |

**Automatic pause triggers:** any two consecutive weeks of FPY decline at a certified gate, overtime above threshold, supplier PPM spike, or any Red Line violation halts compression activity pending MRB review.

---

## 9. The Commercial Stakes

Losing one deal in three on delivery speed against a 6-week competitor is an existential revenue leak, not an operational nuisance. The investment required — long-lead inventory carrying cost, one shift of inspection capacity at bottlenecks, scheduling software, supplier development — is small against recovered win rate, and the quality economics run in your favor: every point of first-pass yield removes rework that consumes both lead time and margin. The competitor at 6 weeks is not braver than you. They are better organized. That is fixable — and unlike the last attempt, this plan gets there by removing the waiting, not by cutting the proof.
